Touring on a classic or retro bike is a decision to prioritise how a journey feels over how efficiently it is completed. And do you know what? On the right roads, that is exactly the right choice. There is something about rolling into a Highland village on a Triumph Bonneville T120, or thumping along a Welsh valley on a Royal Enfield Interceptor 650, that a clinical modern tourer simply cannot replicate. The trick is to accept the bike for what it is and plan around its quirks. Here is how I tour on one and enjoy every mile.

Character is the whole point

Retro bikes are built around a feeling: the lazy torque of a big twin, the sound, the classic lines, the sense that you are riding something with soul. The Moto Guzzi V85 TT arguably splits the difference, wrapping modern touring ability in unmistakable retro character. On a meandering route through the Cornish lanes or over the A44 in mid Wales, where the pleasure is in the pace and the scenery, these bikes are perfect. They ask you to slow down and take it in, which is no bad thing.

Luggage: keep it in the spirit

Modern hard panniers can look out of place on a classic, and the subframes are often not designed for big loads. I go for soft, traditional-looking luggage that suits the bike and respects its limits. A pair of Oxford Heritage Panniers look right and carry enough for a weekend, and a waterproof roll like the Kriega US-10 Drypack handles the overspill. Keep it light. These bikes have modest payloads and older-style suspension that gets flustered by too much weight. Our luggage mounting guide covers how to fit soft luggage securely without a dedicated rack.

Wind protection: from nothing to something

Most retros come with no screen at all, which is charming for a Sunday blast and punishing on a 250-mile day. You do not want a huge touring screen ruining the lines, but a small flyscreen or a neat Puig Retro Screen takes the worst of the blast off your chest while keeping the classic look. It is the difference between arriving relaxed and arriving battered. If you are weighing up screen shapes and sizes for a naked or retro bike, our motorcycle windscreen guide is worth a read.

A retro bike with no wind protection is glorious for an hour and exhausting for five. A small screen is the single upgrade I would never tour without.

British weather being what it is, a set of Oxford Heated Grips is a discreet, period-friendly upgrade that transforms cold mornings over the Lake District passes.

Comfort and ergonomics

The upright, bars-back riding position of most retros is naturally comfortable and easy on the back, which suits touring well. The weak point is usually the seat: flat, firm and styled for looks rather than 300-mile days. An Airhawk Seat Cushion is the fix, or have the seat reshaped if you tour often. Vibration is part of the character on some big twins, so soft grips and a relaxed hold on the bars help on long stints.

Range and fuel strategy

This varies a lot. A modern retro twin like the Interceptor 650 or the Bonneville T120 will happily return 55-65mpg and, with a 12-15 litre tank, give a real-world range of 150-200 miles. Some classics have smaller tanks and thirstier engines, so know your bike before you head into the Highlands. I plan conservatively, treat 130-150 miles as my safe range on a retro, and fill up whenever I pass an open station in remote country. The relaxed pace these bikes encourage actually helps economy.

Pace: ride to the bike's rhythm

Do not fight a classic. These bikes are happiest short-shifting and riding the wave of torque rather than being revved out. Motorways are tolerable but not their happy place; the joy is on the A and B roads where 50-60mph feels fast and involving. Give yourself more time than you would on a modern bike, build in proper stops, and treat the journey as the destination. If you ride with mates on modern machinery, agree regular meeting points rather than trying to hang on.

What to upgrade first

  • A small screen for wind relief.
  • Seat comfort for long days.
  • Heated grips for the British climate.
  • Soft, period-appropriate luggage.
  • Tyres and brakes if the bike is genuinely old; see our touring tyre guide.

Honest limitations

Let us be realistic. Older classics need more mechanical sympathy and a small tool kit; even modern retros are not built for relentless motorway slogging. Payloads and suspension limit how much you can carry, brakes can be modest compared with a modern tourer, and outright weather protection is minimal. Two-up touring with luggage asks a lot of a lightly-sprung retro. None of this is a dealbreaker, but it does shape how and where you tour.

Who it suits

Classic and retro touring is for the rider who values the experience over the stopwatch, who would rather potter through the A5 in Snowdonia soaking it all in than blitz it. It suits shorter, scenic trips beautifully, and with sensible setup a modern retro will happily handle a week away. If you want a bike that turns every fuel stop into a conversation and every mile into a moment, this is the way. For a faster, more clinical all-rounder, our sport tourer playbook makes the opposite case, and both are valid. It just depends what you want from the road.
